title: VantageScore 4.0 Mortgages: What Agents Need to Know
description: VantageScore 4.0 is now open to all Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac lenders. Here's what changed, why buyer scores differ, and how agents can avoid surprises.
image_alt: Two business professionals talking as they walk through a bright modern office hallway

faq.q: Can a homebuyer choose whether the lender uses FICO or VantageScore?
faq.a: No. According to FHFA, the lender chooses Classic FICO or VantageScore 4.0 loan by loan and must use the same model for all borrowers on that loan.

faq.q: Is Classic FICO being retired for mortgages?
faq.a: FHFA says Classic FICO is expected to be retired at a future date, but no retirement date has been announced, and advance notice will be given before any change.

faq.q: Why doesn't my credit app score match my mortgage pre-approval?
faq.a: Consumer apps often show a different scoring model or version and may use one bureau. Mortgage lenders use specific approved models, so the lender's report is the score that counts for the loan.

body_html:
Your buyer checks a credit app, sees one number, and calls you excited. A week later the lender's pre-approval shows a different number. Now your buyer is confused, a little worried, and asking you whether something went wrong.

Usually nothing went wrong. Different credit scores have always existed, and the gap just got more visible. In 2026 the mortgage world started using a second scoring model for conventional loans, and that changes some of the conversations agents have with buyers. Here's what actually changed, what didn't, and how to keep it from becoming a surprise in the middle of a deal.

What Changed With Mortgage Credit Scores in 2026

For decades, loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac relied on older versions of FICO, often called "Classic FICO." That's now shifting. According to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), VantageScore 4.0 began a limited rollout on April 22, 2026, and on September 9, 2026 it opened up to all approved Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac lenders without needing prior written approval.

A few details matter for your buyers:

  • Lenders choose, not borrowers. FHFA says lenders can pick Classic FICO or VantageScore 4.0 loan by loan, but they must use the same model for every borrower on that loan.
  • Classic FICO hasn't gone away. FHFA says it's expected to retire at some point, but no retirement date has been announced.
  • FICO 10T is approved but not yet usable. FHFA notes it is not currently eligible for delivery.
  • Pricing was aligned. FHFA reports that on September 30, 2026, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac adjusted upfront fees so they line up across Classic FICO and VantageScore 4.0.
  • Manual underwriting still uses Classic FICO. A legal summary from Orrick of the September change notes that manually underwritten loans keep using Classic FICO.

On the government side, HUD announced in April 2026 that FHA had accepted VantageScore 4.0 and started implementation, per a joint FHFA and HUD announcement summarized by VantageScore. How and when that shows up varies, so ask your lender how they're handling FHA files today.

Why Your Buyer's Score Might Look Different

Scoring models read the same credit report and weigh it differently. VantageScore describes 4.0 as using trended credit data, meaning it looks at how balances move over time rather than only a single snapshot. Someone who pays down cards every month can look different under that lens than someone who carries a balance, even if their statement balances happen to match on one day.

That's also why the free score in a banking app rarely matches a mortgage pull. Consumer apps often show a different model or version than the one a lender uses, and they may pull from a single bureau. Mortgage credit has traditionally come from all three bureaus.

QuestionClassic FICOVantageScore 4.0
Eligible for Fannie/Freddie loans?YesYes, for all approved lenders since Sept. 9, 2026
Who picks it?The lenderThe lender
Manual underwriting?YesNo, Classic FICO still required
Retirement date?None announcedNot applicable

The practical point: a score is a reading, not a fixed trait. The number that matters is the one the lender actually uses for that loan.

What This Means for Your Offers

For most well-qualified buyers, this change will be invisible. Where it can matter is at the edges, with buyers who are close to a program minimum or a pricing tier, buyers with thin credit files, and buyers who had a recent event like a large balance or a late payment.

That's exactly where agents get burned when a pre-approval is thin. If the lender hasn't actually reviewed the credit, the number in your buyer's head may not be the one that drives the approval. Before you write on a property, it's fair to ask the loan officer a few direct questions:

  1. Did you pull full credit, or is this based on a soft check or what the buyer told you?
  2. Which scoring model is this pre-approval based on?
  3. Is the buyer close to any score cutoff that could change program eligibility or pricing?
  4. Is anything on the report likely to need an explanation letter or follow-up?

A good loan officer will answer those quickly and plainly. If you want a fuller checklist of what to expect from your lending partner, I wrote about that in what great agents should expect from their loan officer.

How to Talk About Credit Without Overpromising

Buyers sometimes hear "new credit score" and assume it means easier approvals. That's not a safe message. A different model can help some files and make no difference for others. Underwriting still looks at income, assets, debts, and the property, and the lender decides which model to use.

Here's language that keeps you on solid ground:

  • "Lenders now have more than one approved way to score credit, so your loan officer will tell you which one applies to your loan."
  • "The score in your app is a helpful signal, but the lender's report is the one that counts."
  • "Let's not open new accounts or run up cards until we close, no matter which score is used."

That last one matters more than any model change. New debt, missed payments, and large balances during escrow still cause problems. For buyers who want to prepare months ahead, my guide on improving your credit score before applying for a mortgage covers the basics.

Where Southern California Buyers Feel It Most

In high-cost markets like Orange County and much of Southern California, small differences in qualification can carry more weight because loan amounts are larger. Many buyers here are also first-generation homeowners, younger professionals, or self-employed borrowers whose credit histories don't always fit a neat pattern.

For those buyers, it helps to work with a lender who looks at the whole file early, explains what the credit report shows, and tells you upfront if there's a soft spot. Surprises at underwriting are what turn a clean escrow into a scramble. The earlier the credit picture is clear, the stronger and more confident the offer.

The Takeaway for Agents

Credit scoring for mortgages is in transition. VantageScore 4.0 is now available to every approved Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac lender, Classic FICO is still in use, and the lender, not the buyer, decides which applies. For your clients, that means one thing above all: the number that matters is the one on the lender's report.

Ask your loan officer which model they used, whether full credit was reviewed, and whether your buyer is near any cutoff. Set expectations without promises. And keep reminding buyers to leave their credit alone until the keys are in hand. If you'd like to talk through how this affects a specific buyer, I'm always glad to take the call.
